subject: Microbiology
subtopic: RNA viruses overview and RNA virus mnemonics
vignette: A student is memorizing which RNA viruses carry positive-sense genomes equivalent to mRNA versus negative-sense genomes that must be transcribed first. She is told to remember the phrase about drinking flavored Corona and eating hippie California pickles.
question: Which of the following groups of viruses all have positive-sense ssRNA genomes?

options.text: Retrovirus, togavirus, flavivirus, coronavirus, hepevirus, calicivirus, picornavirus
Arenavirus, bunyavirus, paramyxovirus, orthomyxovirus, filovirus, rhabdovirus

explanation_correct: Positive-sense ssRNA, which behaves like mRNA and can be translated directly, includes the retro-, toga-, flavi-, corona-, hepe-, calici-, and picornaviruses; the mnemonic is drinking flavored Corona and eating hippie California pickles at a retro toga party. Negative-sense viruses are the arena-, bunya-, paramyxo-, orthomyxo-, filo-, and rhabdoviruses, which must bring their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

explanation_incorrect.A: These are DNA viruses; poxvirus and herpesvirus are dsDNA and hepadnavirus is partially dsDNA.
explanation_incorrect.C: This is exactly the negative-sense list; these virions package RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to make a positive-sense message first.
explanation_incorrect.D: Orthomyxovirus (influenza) and paramyxovirus are negative-sense; reovirus is the one RNA family with dsRNA.
explanation_incorrect.E: Reovirus has a dsRNA genome and rhabdovirus (rabies) is negative-sense ssRNA; neither is positive-sense.

educationalObjective: Positive-sense ssRNA viruses are retro, toga, flavi, corona, hepe, calici, and picornaviruses; negative-sense are arena, bunya, paramyxo, orthomyxo, filo, and rhabdoviruses, which must package polymerase.

subject: Microbiology
subtopic: RNA viruses overview and RNA virus mnemonics
vignette: A first-year student is asked why influenza virus and retrovirus are singled out when learning that RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm. A classmate answers with the phrase retro flu is outta cyt (sight).
question: Which of the following best explains the exceptions to cytoplasmic replication among RNA viruses?

options.text: Both replicate in the cytoplasm but assemble their virions in the nucleus before budding at the plasma membrane
Influenza virus replicates in the nucleus because it requires host splicing machinery, and retrovirus integrates proviral DNA into the host genome in the nucleus
Both replicate exclusively in mitochondria to evade host immunity
Both are DNA viruses misclassified as RNA viruses
Both are naked viruses whose capsids must be disassembled in the nucleus

explanation_correct: All RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm except the retrovirus and influenza virus. Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to make dsDNA, which integrates into the host genome, a nuclear event. Influenza virus, an orthomyxovirus, transcribes and replicates its genome in the nucleus, using host nuclear functions. The mnemonic is Retro flu is outta cyt (sight).

explanation_incorrect.A: Influenza mRNAs are made in the nucleus and retroviral provirus is nuclear DNA; the nuclear step is genome transcription and integration, not merely assembly.
explanation_incorrect.C: Neither virus replicates in mitochondria; influenza uses the host nucleus and retroviruses the host chromosomal DNA.
explanation_incorrect.D: Influenza is an enveloped negative-sense ssRNA orthomyxovirus and HIV is a positive-sense ssRNA retrovirus with reverse transcriptase; neither is a DNA virus.
explanation_incorrect.E: Influenza is enveloped with a helical nucleocapsid and retrovirus is enveloped with an icosahedral core; capsid disassembly location is not the reason for nuclear replication.

educationalObjective: All RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm except influenza virus and retroviruses, which replicate in the nucleus (retro flu is outta cyt).

subject: Microbiology
subtopic: RNA viruses overview and RNA virus mnemonics
vignette: During a review of viral genome architecture, a student is given four RNA virus families and asked to identify which have segmented genomes, remembering the mnemonic BOAR. She is also told that all RNA viruses are single-stranded except one family.
question: Which of the following pairings of RNA virus families with their distinguishing genome features is correct?

options.text: Orthomyxovirus has an unsegmented positive-sense genome
Paramyxovirus has a segmented dsRNA genome
Picornavirus has a fragmented negative-sense genome packaged as multiple segments
Reoviridae is the only dsRNA family, and the segmented families are bunya-, orthomyxo-, arena-, and reoviruses
Flaviviridae has a dsRNA genome and a circular, segmented arrangement

explanation_correct: All RNA viruses have ssRNA genomes except Reoviridae, which has dsRNA, and reovirus is also the rotavirus family that causes infantile gastroenteritis. Segmented genomes occur in the BOAR families: bunya-, orthomyxo-, arena-, and reoviruses. Segmentation matters because it permits reassortment, the mechanism of antigenic shift in influenza.

explanation_incorrect.A: Orthomyxovirus (influenza) is negative-sense and multisegmented, which is precisely why it can reassort and shift.
explanation_incorrect.B: Paramyxoviruses such as measles, mumps, RSV, and parainfluenza are negative-sense and unsegmented ssRNA viruses.
explanation_incorrect.C: Picornaviruses have a single linear positive-sense ssRNA genome translated into one large polyprotein cleaved by viral proteases.
explanation_incorrect.E: Flaviviruses such as hepatitis C, yellow fever, dengue, West Nile, and Zika have linear positive-sense ssRNA genomes and are not segmented.

educationalObjective: Reoviridae is the only dsRNA RNA virus family, and only bunya-, orthomyxo-, arena-, and reoviruses (BOAR) are segmented.
